title: Non-union bands, failing the union test and getting in
summary: Early local bands had no bottom; he flunked his union reading test, then got in when pianist Freddie Small vouched for him.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: So here you were studying with this Czechoslovakian and then starting to work jobs.

That's right. Non-union jobs. We played with a fiddle player. The usual band at that time was a fiddle, MR. GITLER: MR. CHALLIS: a saxophone, no bottom --^N accordinos, ?^N no accordions. Piano, banjo, and drums. Between the drums and the banjo that's where your rhythm came from but there was really no bottom in those bands. The Dixieland Jazz Band did the same thing.

Now, many of the early bands had tubas and occasionally a string bass, bowed. I played around -- well, first of all, I played a lot of these -- several of these non-union jobs and occasionally there was somebody in there that had played with the union guys and they liked what I was doing so they invited me around to take a job.
This is all in Wilkes Barre and the surrounding areas.

This is mostly in Wilkes Barre. Local, quite local. I was 15, 16 years old. I was really the kid among kids and I was at it all the time, and I mean I enjoyed it and if I weren't com-pahs thumping them with the record out there at the piano, where I got, I imagine a lot of my harmonies. There they were very plain. Plain chords the seventh seldom went beyond seventh, No or ninths elevenths or anything like that. That had to come later.
Did you start improvising on the C-Melody?
Oh, yes, it was all improvising. As a matter of fact, I couldn't read. I flunked my union test,

because I couldn't read. My teacher was on the board and he wouldn't do a thing for me, and then I played with a guy that came around that later played with the Scranton Sirens, a fellow by the name of Fred Smalls and he was a piano player and he had an orchestra and he was quite a piano player and he had drums, banjo, violin and occasionally bass, which I liked.

I liked that bottom. They had a man around there who could play em short. This is before the pizzicato. He was bowing. It was all bow then and some of them just bowed so long, it didn't make any difference to me whether they were there or not. But this one particular guy, he would shorten it up to where he gave a little beat to it, a little rhythm.

This piano player, he had trouble with his saxophone player and the saxophone player, I guess he didn't pay him. The saxophone player took him to the union, so I went down to the union for my second examination and it happened to be at the same time that he was being tried, so he asked the union 'If he's having problems -- he said he can't get a saxophone player,' how about if I used this kid?'
So they said okay. And that's how I got in the union.
Kind of start learning on the job.
Yes. I learned as I played.
